speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: It connects us to the world and anchors our status as a global hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: As we continue to grow, we want to do so sustainably, so that future generations of Singaporeans can also experience the joy of air travel and Singapore can continue to serve as a premier air hub for the region and the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) has set a long-term aspirational goal of net zero carbon emissions for international aviation by 2050.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: As a member of the international civil aviation community and an ICAO Council Member, we are committed to working towards that goal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: We will do so in a practical manner, advancing both sustainability and competitiveness, not one at the expense of the other.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: The Singapore Sustainable Air Hub Blueprint was launched last year and sets out Singapore’s approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Within this, the implementation of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) is a critical pathway for us to realise our aviation decarbonisation goals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: This Bill provides the legislative framework to enable its adoption in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: SAF is the most practical way to decarbonise aviation today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: It is a drop-in fuel that can be blended with jet fuel, for use with existing aircraft and refuelling infrastructure, without the need for costly modifications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: SAF is expected to contribute around 65% of the carbon emission reduction needed by aviation to achieve net zero by 2050.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Recognising the importance of SAF to aviation decarbonisation, ICAO and its member states have agreed to a collective global aspirational vision to reduce international aviation emissions by five percent by 2030 through the use of SAF and other cleaner energies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: However, there are challenges in the adoption of SAF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Number two, on the demand side, uptake is uneven and often concentrated in regions with strong mandates or subsidies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Number three, the sector is still nascent, and the costs remain high and volatile.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Currently, SAF costs about three to four times more than conventional jet fuel.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Countries around the world have taken different approaches.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: They require fuel suppliers to blend SAF into conventional jet fuel.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: The European Union's (EU’s) ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation, for instance, requires a two percent SAF blend by 2025, rising progressively to 70% by 2050.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: The United Kingdom's (UK’s) SAF mandate targets a 10% blend by 2030.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: They are exploring a revenue certainty mechanism to encourage investment in SAF production.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: This includes a guaranteed minimum level of revenue for SAF producers, even when market prices fluctuate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: In the United States (US), federal incentives as well as state-level programmes help to lower the cost of SAF and encourage domestic production.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: We have studied these approaches for Singapore carefully.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Both have their merits, but they also come with trade-offs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Due to price volatility, mandates create significant cost uncertainty for airlines and passengers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: In adopting SAF, we want to provide cost certainty to airlines and passengers and ensure that the cost is manageable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Subsidies, on the other hand, require large and recurring fiscal commitments, which are not fiscally sustainable for Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Singapore has therefore chosen a pragmatic and balanced approach, calibrated to our circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: We do this in three ways: through a SAF target, fixed cost envelope model and centralised procurement approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: We have consulted the industry and assessed that starting with a 1% target is manageable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: It will not increase air ticket prices significantly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: On the other hand, the 1% target will send a firm demand signal to the market to spur production and industry development in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: It allows us to do our part to support aviation decarbonisation, while laying the groundwork for broader adoption in the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: At the same time, cost certainty is critical.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: SAF is still a nascent product that is subject to high price volatility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Unlike fossil jet fuel, airlines cannot hedge the price of SAF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Under this model, the total amount spent on SAF each year will be pre-determined based on our SAF target and the projected SAF premium.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: The amount needed will be collected upfront via the SAF levy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Instead, SAF uplift volumes will be adjusted accordingly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: This ensures cost certainty for airlines, passengers and shippers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: This allows us to secure better commercial terms with fuel suppliers and ensures that the levy proceeds are used in an accountable and effective manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: It helps to encourage SAF production through clear demand signals, while ensuring that costs remain contained, predictable and fairly shared.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: These in turn allow us to meet our environmental responsibilities while safeguarding the competitiveness of our air hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: The airports in Singapore that require the payment of SAF levy will be as specified in an Order made by the Minister for Transport.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: The Order may also provide for other details, such as different amounts or rates that may be imposed in respect of different classes of passengers, cargoes, airports or aircraft.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 3 of the Bill amends section 7(1) to create a new function for CAAS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: CAAS may procure, manage, account for and allocate SAF and SAF environmental attributes, or establish and appoint a company to carry out these functions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: SAF environmental attributes (SAF EAs) represent the difference in carbon dioxide emissions between the same quantities of SAF and conventional aviation fuel throughout their respective life cycles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Under the Bill, the SAF and SAF EAs may be allocated to persons who pay SAF levies or any other person as prescribed in an Order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 5 of the Bill inserts new sections 25C and 25D.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Clauses 6, 7 and 8 make miscellaneous amendments to sections 86, 87 and 87A to align the provisions on the aviation levy and airport development levy with the new section 87B for consistency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: This Bill is an important enabler of Singapore's aviation decarbonisation journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: It reflects Singapore’s commitment to international decarbonisation goals and our determination to pursue a pragmatic and balanced approach that supports the competitiveness of our Singapore air hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: We will continue to work closely with the aviation industry and stakeholders to ensure the smooth implementation of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The intent behind these amendments to decarbonise aviation and align Singapore with the global net-zero targets is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The global aviation sector is at a crossroads.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While SAF offers a promising pathway to decarbonisation, it is still in its infancy in terms of supply, cost and scalability.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The question before us is how we get there, and at what pace and price.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To this end, I would like to raise a few points for clarification.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, on the viability of SAF, both economically and technologically.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, on upstream capacity and whether global supply can meet our ambitions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Third, on feedstock availability and type, given regional constraints.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fourth, the impact of the levy on investors and airlines.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And finally, on regional opportunities – how this transition could create green jobs and help Singapore leapfrog as a regional hub for sustainable aviation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: SAF is the aviation industry's best near-term pathway to decarbonisation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This raises the question of just how economically and technologically viable SAF is.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Without sufficient scale, a SAF levy risks becoming a cost burden on airlines and passengers rather than a market signal strong enough to catalyse real change.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Norway and the EU, SAF blending mandates have been introduced.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Norway, 0.5% blending requirement, implemented in 2020, did increase SAF uptake, but at significant cost to carriers, which in turn led to ticket price increases and logistical complexities in supply.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Similarly, the EU's RefuelEU Aviation regulation, passed this year, mandated a progressive SAF blend rising to 70% by 2050.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, the European Commission itself acknowledges that high production costs remain the biggest constraint.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The energy transition toward carbon neutrality demands a transformation across the entire aviation supply chain, from producers to off-takers, from regulators to the flying public.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is not a change that one sector can shoulder alone.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It requires a shared understanding of how costs and upstream investments are borne, how responsibilities are shared and how each phase of implementation unfolds.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For a SAF levy to truly succeed, it must inspire confidence, de-risk investment and drive down costs over time.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Globally, even major energy players, such as Shell and BP, have slowed or paused SAF investment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Without strong market guarantees or co-investment frameworks, smaller producers will not invest in new refineries or feedstock supply chains.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore's SAF levy could be made more effective by pairing it with targeted incentives, such as joint ventures or green finance instruments like transition bonds, to support feedstock aggregation and upstream infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Japan's "ACT FOR SKY" consortium offers a useful model, where the government united airlines, fuel suppliers and trading houses to co-invest in early-stage SAF projects, aligning public and private risk to achieve scale.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The success of SAF depends very much on the feedstock, which is the raw material used to produce it.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, most SAF comes from things like used cooking oil, animal fats, or farm waste.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A McKinsey study found that by 2030, such waste-based sources can meet only about 30% of global demand.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The rest will have to come from more advanced fuels made using captured carbon and green hydrogen – technologies that are still expensive and developing.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To build Singapore's position as a sustainable aviation hub, we must look closely at what kinds of feedstock are available in our region.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Broadly, there are two types: first-generation feedstock is made from food crops such as corn, sugarcane, or palm oil.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second-generation feedstock is made from waste materials such as used cooking oil or animal fat.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, when you take into account the clearing of land to grow palm oil, the total carbon pollution from palm oil-based fuel can actually be higher than regular jet fuel, more than 100 grammes of CO₂ per unit of energy, compared to about 89 grammes for conventional jet fuel.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In contrast, fuels made from used cooking oil or animal fat can reduce emissions by 60% to 70%, because they use recycle existing waste rather than grow new crops.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The problem is that these waste materials are limited and already in demand by other industries.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That is why international bodies like ICAO, through its Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) framework, now define which feedstocks truly count as sustainable.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some, like palm oil residues, are still hotly debated because of concerns about deforestation and how carbon is measured.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Choosing the wrong mix of feedstocks could hurt both our environmental goals and economic opportunities in the carbon market.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Alternatively, a more practical approach could be to set uniform emissions targets, adjusted according to each feedstock's carbon intensity, so that producers are rewarded for using cleaner inputs and held accountable for those with higher carbon intensities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For investors developing refineries, feedstock logistics, or synthetic fuel technologies, such uncertainty poses a challenge.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Manufacturing operations require a minimum scale to be viable.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The SAF levy rightly internalises environmental costs and encourages greener choices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore could consider a similar approach, such as a performance-linked rebate or co-investment scheme, where part of the levy revenues is directed into SAF research and development (R&D), production infrastructure, or feedstock aggregation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would create a more circular levy and crucially, send a strong signal of long-term policy confidence to investors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another avenue is to enable voluntary contributions, especially from corporate travellers, to fund SAF adoption.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would expand financing options and engage the public in Changi's sustainability journey.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ultimately, producers need predictability, in terms of off-take volumes to justify investments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The current levy provides price certainty, but it risks volume volatility.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Despite these challenges, Sir, there are promising opportunities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With strategic design, the SAF levy could put us in the lead as a regional hub for SAF, attracting new green investments, encouraging co-location of upstream production facilities, creating high-value jobs across the feedstock, refining and carbon management value chains.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given our established petrochemical expertise and proximity to Southeast Asia's agricultural base, Singapore is uniquely positioned to coordinate feedstock-to-fuel supply chains.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A collaborative framework with Association for Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) partners could enable joint certification, financing and trade of SAF across borders, much like how Singapore pioneered regional liquefied natural gas (LNG) trading.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond serving as a trading and refining hub, Singapore can also derive direct benefits from co-locating SAF production and carbon management activities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would generate quality employment in advanced manufacturing, logistics and sustainability services, and anchor Singapore in the upstream value chain, from feedstock aggregation and processing to downstream carbon credit generation through verified emission reductions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have raised clarifications on five areas: one, the viability of SAF; two, upstream production capacity; three, feedstock standards; four, investment certainty; and five, regional opportunities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, how the Ministry plans to support upstream development, ensure off-take stability for producers and grow high-value jobs and local enterprise opportunities through this transition.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With clear policies and strong partnerships, Singapore can turn this levy into a catalyst for green aviation leadership.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The production of SAF is still nascent and breakthroughs may come in sparse so Singapore must stay agile to capitalise on them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With our worldclass logistics trade links and existing refinery presence, we are well-placed to lead in the regional SAF industry.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We can build flexibility into our SAF regimes so that when new pathways mature, we can scale up quickly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We believe it is important to tackle carbon emissions from international aviation even if they are not covered under Singapore's national carbon budget.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is because it is the right thing to do.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is an area where we have a measure of control and it is a move that will benefit our economy and society in the long run by future-proofing our status as an international aviation hub.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Generally, the new provisions in the Bill allow for a more straightforward and policy stable approach to SAF adoption.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Nevertheless, I have some clarifications to seek from the Minister of State regarding the mechanics and implications of this legislation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My queries fall broadly into the following categories: one, the rationale and transparency of the proposed SAF fund mechanism; two, issues of process regarding the implementation of the fund; three, the impact of the new levy on travellers and the broader strategy of fair decarbonisation of Singapore's aviation sector and; four, ensuring that we remain ready to scale and capture market share as the technology develops.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I note this is different from the funding mechanism in say, the EU or the UK.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Why not allow the cost to be passed through directly and transparently by the airlines?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Is the fund primarily intended as a risk-pooling mechanism, or does it serve another strategic purpose?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is stated that the fund will not form part of the CAAS revenue and will also be used for administrative cost.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Furthermore, does the Government have any projections yet on the annual total collections via the levy?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This information is vital for public accountability and for assessing the efficiency and scale of this new policy tool.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Two, issues of process for the implementation of the SAF procurement mechanism.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I turn to the issues of process regarding the implementation of the procurement mechanism, it is not entirely clear from the Bill who or what will be the procuring entity mentioned in clause 5, which outlines the purposes of the SAF fund.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Currently, there is only one major SAF operator in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Given that we have ambitions to scale up the sector, how can new players be assured that the procurement process is fair and open to all?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister, what is the timeline for the formal establishment and operationalisation of this procuring entity?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the interim before the entity is formally set up, is the CAAS the designated procuring entity?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How is the procuring entity going to be appointed and governed?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will its structure be similar to existing models such as the Singapore Gas Co Ptd Ltd under the Energy Market Authority?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will private sector firms be involved in this procuring entity?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Regardless of whether it is a wholly owned, public or mixed entity, will the procuring entity be subject to the standard public agency procurement rules to ensure fair and competitive processing of SAF?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, our neighbours in Malaysia, Indonesia and Australia, produce or are capable of producing large volumes of feedstock.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We have healthy trade relationships with many economies in the region and we should consider establishing a cooperative framework that can ensure a steady supply of feedstock into our facilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Having a clear and fair framework for regional cooperation will also strengthen Singapore's status as a leader in the carbonisation efforts in the region.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some have significant significantly higher greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions due to inefficient conversion, higher carbon cost at production or polluting by-products.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must ensure that we do not inadvertently become a tool for green washing in our quest to be a leader in the nascent SAF industry.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We can perhaps strengthened safeguards by defining categories of feedstock acceptable under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, the impact on travellers and fair decarbonisation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is set against the context that Singapore already charges fairly high airport fees, for example, due to the Terminal 5 development levy, otherwise known as the Airport Development Levy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On the issue of financial impact on travellers, I have the following questions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A clear illustration is helpful to manage public expectations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Is the Bill designed to simply allow airlines the discretion to decide how these new costs are passed down to different classes or passengers at least in terms of cost?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A flat rate imposition could disproportionately affect those travelling in economy class.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the Minister also provide some information on the way SAF levy charges will apply for outbound air cargo?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would like the Minister to elaborate on the expected impact of this levy and fund on the development of Singapore's domestic SAF industry and its overall supply.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to ask whether the industry is currently constrained primarily by a lack of guaranteed demand from airlines, or is this levy needed more because it will provide the financial support necessary for the industry to overcome the technological and cost challenges of producing SAF?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I note that IATA recently released a study suggesting the main bottleneck is more with technology rather than the availability of feedstocks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We have used cooking oil, being the main commercially available process.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the Government's view, how far is the industry from commercially scaling up other crucial processes such as power to liquid SAF?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I asked this because if our ability to make aviation feel more sustainable is still constrained by technological or supply side limitation, we must also think more broadly about reducing emissions through other viable means.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This includes reducing per passenger emissions by encouraging airlines to adopt higher passenger density on the aircraft, albeit carefully drawing appropriate balance between basic acceptable comfort and numbers, especially for the economy class.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Expert groups, such as the Global Solidarity Levies Task Force has suggested that this could be achieved by raising fees on classes with lower passenger density, such as business or first class, as well as on private jet passengers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such a policy structure would align the cost of travel more closely with the environmental impact and promote a fairer distribution of the decarbonisation burden.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But this increases operating costs for airlines, which are then typically passed on to passengers as higher ticket price.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This situation creates a risk of carbon leakage, which is commonly understood as the increase in emissions outside a region imposing a climate policy due to businesses or consumers shifting their activities to areas with less stringent regulations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In aviation this leakage may happen when airlines or passengers avoid the levy by hard switching.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: That is to say, they opt for connecting flights to international airports that do not impose the SAF charge, thereby displacing the carbon intensive activity rather than truly reducing global emissions and putting the regulated hub at the competitive disadvantage.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Singapore is spearheading the development of SAFs in the region with Neste's Tuas facility, the first of its kind globally, marking a significant step forward.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Government has made clear its intent to continue advancing SAF as a key pillar of Singapore's sustainable aviation strategy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However in a nascent and rapidly evolving industry, technological breakthroughs are unpredictable and can often occur in bursts rather than along a steady trajectory.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It empowers CAAS to review these from time to time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What should trigger future changes to the levy or SAF target?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Should adjustment depend on global supply milestones, declining price differentials or broader regional capacity developments?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I know the Senior Minister of State has explained on this.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Nevertheless, let me suggest, to ensure flexibility and market alignment, Singapore could adopt a trigger base framework where each revision is activated only when specific verifiable conditions are met.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Alternatively, escalation could be tied to regional production capacity or carbon intensity benchmarks verified under ICAO's CORSIA framework.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such an approach ensures that taxpayers and airlines can be confident that adjustments are implemented only when the market is ready, keeping Singapore nimble and responsive to dynamic global conditions rather than bound to an arbitrary timeline.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am heartened that Singapore is taking tangible first steps in line with the global aviation industry's goals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Of course, this must only be the beginning and we should and must explore further avenues for fair and effective decarbonisation after this.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I look forward to the Minister of State's clarifications on the questions I have raised.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: My Deputy Speaker, I declare my interest as an employee in the aviation sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This is a price which every departing passenger has to pay and while it may be a small amount, it is one in which consumers have no choice in, have no control over, in terms of adapting their behaviours to the change in price and actually, from which they enjoy no benefit, except indirectly.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In my speech, I will request for clarifications on three points: one, why is the cost burden levied solely on passengers; two, will SAF levy rate increase in the future and; three, is the central procurement model necessarily the most cost-effective.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The global aviation sector is responsible for about 3% of global carbon emissions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In 2024, Changi Airport reported 1.207 million tonnes of CO2 emissions, which is about 2% of Singapore’s carbon emission and only 0.13% share of CO2 emissions from global aviation, or only 0.0039% of global CO2 emissions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: As Singapore has only one international airport, estimated at 0.0039%, our effective contribution to global carbon emissions is actually very small.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Nevertheless, as a key leader in global aviation and Singapore Changi Airport being a leading regional and international air hub, we must do our part to support global efforts in sustainable aviation and meet ICAO's Net Zero goal by 2050.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In the recent ICAO Assembly, a collective global aspirational vision to reduce CO2 emissions in international aviation by 5% by 2030 was adopted.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In fact, several airports and jurisdictions have already implemented mandatory SAF policies.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: For instance, the European Aviation Security Agency (EASA) has mandated, since January this year, a minimum 2% blend on Aviation Fuel Suppliers in European Union (EU) airports.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Their long-term target is to increase to 70% blend by 2050.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: At the same time, airlines, such as KLM and Delta Airlines, have pledged a 10% SAF blend by 2030, while industry bodies, such as IATA's Fly Net Zero roadmap, lean on SAF for 65% of all emission cuts by 2050.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: At the same time, it is the airlines which will benefit from the carbon credits that accrue from the use of these clean fuels.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: It is, therefore, the airlines, and not the consumer, who should be the object of taxes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In many countries and jurisdictions, the cost of SAF is indeed directly borne by airlines or by aviation fuel suppliers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Hence, the first question is, why do passengers and not the airlines pay?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Second, why does the Government even need to mandate a SAF levy on passengers, when some airlines have already voluntarily committed to decarbonisation through SAF for their corporate decarbonisation targets?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Some airlines have also signed up on the CORSIA framework under ICAO, to reduce their carbon footprint.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: If I may draw an analogy, it is akin to restaurants using styrofoam packaging, and the Government wanting them to switch to green packaging.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: And rather than levying taxes on those restaurants using styrofoams, the Government has decided to tax the diners instead.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Further, this tax is not only on diners at restaurants with styrofoam packaging, but on all diners, even those dining at establishments that are already using green packaging.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This is, to say the least, a very odd state of affairs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I hope the Minister can clarify why is Singapore's approach different from all other countries in the world.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Was there public engagement with passengers on the imposition of the SAF levy?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Also, can the Minister clarify if there is a plan to roll back on the SAF levy if more airlines are voluntarily committing to decarbonisation?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This is a small step in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In 2024, Changi Airport contributed only 0.13% to global aviation's carbon emissions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: With a 3% to 5% SAF blend, what is the effectiveness in reducing the global aviation's carbon emissions?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In order for Singapore to contribute more meaningfully to ICAO's Net Zero by 2050 goal, do we expect a steady increase in the SAF blend requirement above 5% after 2030?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: If so, will the SAF levy, correspondingly, increase in the future?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Currently, SAF is two to five times more expensive than Jet A-1 fuel.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: As demand for SAF increases, the cost may also increase, if supply of feedstock continues to be limited.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: If the revenue from levy collected is insufficient to cope with the SAF price increase, will the SAF levy be expected to increase in the future?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This makes Singapore the largest producer of the renewable jet fuel in the world.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The expanded facility is owned and operated by Finnish energy company, Neste.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: With Neste being the only SAF producer in Singapore, how does SAFCo then ensure that SAF procured is most cost effective?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: How will SAFCo bring more producers in to increase competition?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Currently, airlines have their own teams that will procure Jet A-1 fuel.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Many airlines hedge forward fuel prices and some, which predict the trend wrongly, may turn airlines into huge losses.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: SAF is just one of the many ways to decarbonise the industry.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: While we get started on SAF operations, we should also keep an open mind on other viable options along the way.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: More countries than ever, including our neighbours, such as Indonesia, have pledged to incorporate SAFs into their aviation industries.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (Amendment) Bill, therefore, aims to aid Singapore towards this endeavour.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: On this Bill, I have two questions: first, the risks of the SAF market; and second, the levy impact on consumers while we maintain our competitiveness as an aviation hub.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: My first question really touches on the risk of investing in the SAF market, which is a novel market, subject to high uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The new sections 25C and 25D proposed in the Bill state that the Authority may use the SAF fund to carry out investments.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The net income of the fund is calculated by an addition or reduction from the income derived from investments.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill also accounts for instances where such investments could lead to losses.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: A big concern in the SAF industry is in its novelty stage, especially in second generation SAF processes, which are not yet proven to be commercially viable.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The success of these projects is uncertain, whereby the costs of failed ventures are largely incurred by investors and in this case, the SAF fund.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, the SAF fund is inherently risky as the SAF industry is still in an early stage and profits may be vulnerable to sudden changes in technological advancements, viability of second generation SAFs and policies of other countries.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, will the SAF fund invest in the second generation SAF industry?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Second, on levy impact on consumers and maintaining competitiveness as an aviation hub.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore is fortunate enough that we can afford to expend more to protect the environment and the levies and funds set out in clause 9 of the Bill today would certainly assist us in affording this transition towards SAFs.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: However, air travel in Singapore is already considerably expensive for regular consumers.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: And how does the Government plan to maintain Singapore's competitiveness and perhaps, also harmonise standards as an aviation hub, given that other regional airports may not impose a similar levy?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is a forward-looking and pragmatic piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill does more than establish the SAF fund and levy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It gives us a clear, stable framework to turn our Sustainable Air Hub Blueprint from aspiration into action.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But this Bill is not just about planes or policies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about families planning their next holiday.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about the thousands of Singaporeans whose livelihoods depend on our position as a trusted global air hub.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, the question before us is this: how do we fly toward a greener future without losing our altitude as a competitive, connected economy?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To that end, I wish to seek clarifications on five key areas: transparency, fairness, competitiveness, accountability and international alignment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, predictability builds trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singaporeans can accept modest green contributions when they understand what they are paying for.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But a green cost must be a seen cost, not one hidden in the fine print.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Section 87B of the Bill rightly requires that if a levy is passed on, the amount must be stated.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the implementing order require the SAF levy to appear as a clear, separate line item on all passenger tickets and cargo contracts?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It should never be buried inside a "taxes and fees" bundle.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And will the Ministry consider codifying a cap in subsidiary legislation, so that families can plan with confidence?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will short-, medium- and long-haul be defined – by distance or flight time?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister of State ensure that cargo levies are transparently itemised in freight contracts, instead of being rolled into "all-in" rates?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This transparency gives our small exporters the clarity to price their goods competitively and hold logistics partners accountable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, for this levy to be legitimate, it must also be fair.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Those who contribute more to carbon emissions should bear a proportionate share of the cost.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill's powers for differentiation and remission under section 87B are, therefore, crucial.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Globally, there is a growing call for fairness in climate policy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Studies show that a small fraction of frequent flyers and premium travellers account for a disproportionately large share of aviation emissions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many countries are exploring progressive levies to address that imbalance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore should not shy away from this conversation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, essential flights, such as humanitarian missions, medical evacuations or pilot training, should rightly be exempted.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry publish clear exemption criteria, so operators are not left guessing in an emergency?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will it also disclose, annually, how many exemptions were granted and why, so the public can see fairness in action?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For SMEs facing urgent cargo needs, will there be a defined remission process, especially when cost pressures or timing make the levy burdensome?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about ensuring no one is penalised for trying to do the right thing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, our air hub is the heartbeat of our economy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Tens of thousands of Singaporeans, pilots, engineers, caterers, cleaners, depend on it every day.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Section 87B specifies that the levy applies to flights taking off from Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are the lifeblood of Changi's success and essential to its competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must also guard against what some have called "green fatigue".

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Around the world, passengers and politicians are showing signs of giving up on greener air travel, weary of rising costs, divided politics and confusing regulations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore cannot afford to be part of that retreat.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must show that ambition and accountability can co-exist.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That is why the timing and design of this levy matter.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Likewise, with sustainable fuel procurement mandated, will budget carriers with thinner margins struggle to operate here?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could that affect connectivity and affordability for travellers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry consider publishing a multi-year levy schedule, setting out indicative rates for the next three to five years?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A transparent roadmap will give both households and businesses the confidence to plan ahead.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For cargo operators, can the Minister of State ensure that levies are structured with stable, geography-based rates and weight bands?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That clarity will help our small and medium enterprises (SMEs) maintain Singapore's reputation as a reliable logistics hub.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, every green dollar must now show its work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singaporeans will support this levy only if they know each cent is used responsibly and effectively to make our skies cleaner.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The creation of a ring-fenced SAF fund under section 25C is the right step forward.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What key performance indicators (KPIs) will the SAF Procuring Entity be measured against, competitive pricing, source diversification and maximising physical uplift at Changi?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: SAF currently accounts for less than 1% of global jet fuel consumption.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That is why Singapore's approach must be pragmatic, scaling gradually, aggregating demand and building credibility step by step.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, when sourcing SAF, can we ensure that Singapore's investment strengthens domestic and regional capabilities, building our own production base, where feasible, and positioning local firms within the green aviation value chain?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, this Bill must also work hand-in-hand with international frameworks, especially CORSIA.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singaore already mandates monitoring and reporting through the Air Navigation Regulations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we have not yet legislated the offsetting duties or penalties for non-compliance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Without enforcement, compliant airlines pay their fair share while others may get a free ride.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: More importantly, passengers risk being double-charged, once under the SAF levy and again under separate CORSIA-related offsets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If countries fail to coordinate their climate measures, consumers lose trust and the green agenda falters.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry ensure that any CORSIA-related costs passed to consumers are clearly displayed as a separate line item, distinct from the SAF levy, to prevent confusion or duplication?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And finally, will the framework apply only to flights between states that are CORSIA-participants, so our carriers remain aligned with global norms and remain competitive?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It asks us to see sustainability not as a cost, but as an investment, in our future, in our children and in our planet.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It asks our families to do their part, our businesses to innovate and our Government to lead with integrity and foresight.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have spoken about transparency, so Singaporeans can see where every dollar goes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have spoken about fairness, so the burden is shared justly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have spoken about competitiveness, so our air hub remains strong in a turbulent world.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have spoken about accountability, so trust in our system remains unshakable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And we have spoken about alignment, so Singapore continues to lead by example on the global stage.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But beyond all that, this Bill challenges us to look skyward and ask: how do we build a future where progress does not come at the planet's expense?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Around the world, some are giving up on greener air travel.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They say the politics are too hard, the costs too high and the people too weary.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must show that realism and resolve can walk hand-in-hand, that we can fly further because we choose to fly cleaner.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we get this right, Singapore will not just be a world-class air hub.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We will be a trusted one, known for doing the right thing, even when it is not the easy thing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us move forward with clear eyes, steady hands and open skies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us keep Singapore flying high, not just in the air, but in our ideals.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The first is on the financial structure of the levy.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As this levy is passed on to consumers, we need clear assurance that their contribution is both effective and monitored.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would be grateful if the Minister of State could inform the House of the specific mechanisms and reporting protocols.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: CAAS was established to actively monitor these estimates and ensure that actual financial impact of the levy on ticket prices remains predictable and consistently aligns with the Ministry's initial projections.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A crucial point for public confidence is technical basis for the cost difference.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could the Minister of State provide more detailed elaboration on the methodology, including the specific fossil fuel benchmark used to assess how the cost of the banded fuel of jet fuel was calculated and substantiated to be more than three times that of Jet Propellant 8 (JP-8) fuel?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore is a major refining hub, home to significant self-production capacity, such as Neste's expanded facility.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Minister's assurance is sought on the strategy for how the presence of these advanced facilities will be utilised to bring the cost of SAF lower over time, rather than merely acting as a platform for centralised procurement and persistently high global market rates.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This SAF levy is a public contribution towards a critical national goal and the accompanying trust must be transparently maintained.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While the blueprint indicates the fund will purchase SAF at its actual market price, the Bill is not explicit on public reporting obligations.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I urge to consider establishing a clear formal reporting obligation for CAAS regarding the SAF Fund.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the Ministry commit to publish a regular and comprehensive report for the public?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such a report should document the total levy collected and expended, the volume and cost of SAF purchase, the actual SAF uplift proportion achieved by airlines and, most importantly, the measurable environmental impact and carbon emissions reduction delivered by the fund.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I commend the Ministry for this decisive step towards the long-term decarbonisation for our aviation industry.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, Deputy Speaker, Sir, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The levy will also help airlines in Changi Airport meet CORSIA requirements, the global carbon reduction scheme for international aviation which will become mandatory in 2027.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Climate change is a major threat, especially for us, a tiny, low-lying island at the equator.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must do our part, not only for ourselves but also for our future generations.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: However, notwithstanding my support, I must voice a few caveats and seek some clarifications or, rather, reassurances, from the Minister.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Allow me to share some quick numbers with the House.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This total sum is significantly higher than those of competing air hubs in the region.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We have strong values in connectivity, efficiency and quality of service.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Of course, I do not believe that we can successfully compete on cost and perhaps, nor should we.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: However, our current passenger fees are already higher than all of our regional competitors.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: If costs rise too much, surely, we risk undermining Changi's position as a global air hub.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Other airports are working hard to beat us at our own game.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: They are learning from us, improving on both hardware and software.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Notably, none of our peer competitors, such as Incheon and Dubai airports, are as expensive.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: If we are not careful, if we take our eyes off the ball, someone else will be stealing our lunch.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Next, I note that the proposed amendments enable a levy on both passenger and cargo flights.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I shall not pre-empt the detailed announcement of the levy structure.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We do have some sense of how the centralised levy will work for passengers and a ballpark figure for the initial rate.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: However, there is still little detail on how the levy mechanism will apply to cargo flights.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is also a key cargo hub in the Asia Pacific.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Beyond pure cargo flights, many services are hybrids, carrying both passengers and freight.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: For them, intangibles, such as the Changi experience or the sights of Jewel have absolutely no bearing.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In that regard, cargo operators will even be more sensitive to increases in levies and costs.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The impact could also be more significant to them in absolute dollar terms, since freight consignments can be much larger than individual tickets.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: That is how equitable the levy system is.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The size of the levy quantum will be of great concern to cargo operators.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It will directly impact Singapore's standing as a leading cargo hub.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It connects Singapore to the rest of the world.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It also supports a large number of jobs, both directly and indirectly.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The success of our air hub is crucial importance to our country.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must ensure that it remains strong and competitive.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I am glad to know that the CAAS Sustainable Air Hub Blueprint, was recognised that environmental sustainability must be balanced with competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The previous Minister for Transport had also repeatedly emphasised the same point in this House.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There is no benefit in moving too far ahead of others in SAF adoption.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Sustainability and competitiveness must go hand in hand.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Only when we maintain our competitiveness, only when we thrive, can we meaningfully pursue sustainability goals.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Without economic strength, sustainability becomes a heavy burden and a constraint.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But I hope the Minister can assure us that cost structures are being closely monitored and that our air hub will remain competitive even as we pursue sustainability goals.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must always remind ourselves that sustainability and economic competitiveness must be pursued together.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Globally, air passenger traffic is projected by IATA to double by 2040, driven by a growing middle class and rising regional connectivity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Asia Pacific will lead this expansion and as a major global air hub, Singapore is well placed to capture a significant share of this growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This will reinforce Singapore's position as a leading global air hub for the future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This growth will not only strengthen air connectivity, but also catalyse growth across tourism, logistics, hospitality, retail, e-commerce and urban development.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It will power our aerospace sector, a key pillar of our manufacturing base.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Today, Singapore accounts for over 10% of global maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) output, and for engine MRO, it accounts for close to 20% of global market share; a position earned through decades of trust and capability.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They reflect how deeply aviation is woven into our economic fabric.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A strong aviation sector anchors growth, attracts investment, drives innovation and creates good jobs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Supporting it is not only an economic policy, it is a strategic necessity for Singapore's continued prosperity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The industry recognises this challenge and is taking major steps to reduce its environmental impact.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: New-generation aircraft, such as, the Airbus A350 powered by Trent XWB engines, achieve up to 25% lower fuel burn and CO2 emissions through better aerodynamics, advanced materials and efficient propulsion.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And the fleet renewal is supporting this transition.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Under the ECLIF3 programme, Airbus, Rolls Royce and the German Aerospace Centre successfully tested 100% SAF on both engines of an A350, demonstrating its compatibility and emissions benefits.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Here in Singapore, CAAS' Sustainable Air Hub Blueprint sets out our roadmap towards net-zero aviation emissions by 2050, focusing on SAF adoption, electrification of ground operations and renewable energy deployment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These efforts show that aviation growth and sustainability are not mutually exclusive.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As a leading global hub, Singapore can prove that responsible aviation growth and climate stewardship can go hand in hand.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: However, as we advance this important goal, we must take a balanced approach, recognising both its strategic advantages and practical implications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I wish to raise three clarifications: firstly, how Singapore will ensure SAF supplies stability and manage price volatility while investing sufficiently in future production; secondly, how we will safeguard Singapore's competitiveness as an air hub amid regional expansion; and thirdly, how we will ensure fairness and equity in how the cost of transition is shared across passengers and industry stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Decarbonising aviation is essential, but the transition must also be economically and operationally sustainable for airlines, passengers and industry players.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Neste's expanded refinery in Tuas now produces more than one million tonnes of SAF annually, making it one of the largest facilities in the world and positioning Singapore as a key node in the regional SAF value chain.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: However, other countries are rapidly increasing capacity too.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In our region, EcoCeres Renewable Fuels and Petronas are developing similar facilities targeting about one million tonnes per year.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: With rising global demand and new mandates, such as, in France, Sweden and Japan requiring 10% SAF blending by 2030, we can expect increased competition for feedstock and price volatility.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Hence, my first clarification: how will Singapore manage this volatility?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: What measures will ensure stability in ticket pricing and airline operations, especially when market fluctuates?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is in addition to the levy that has already been imposed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Based on 2024 Changi Airport passenger volumes of 67.7 million passengers, this could generate at least a minimum $210 million annually; a meaningful start.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But will the fund be sufficient to not only procure SAF, but to also develop local production capacity, support R&D and also diversify feedstocks?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How will this fund be aligned across agencies, like CAAS, the Economic Development Board and Enterprise Singapore, to build an end-to-end resilient SAF supply-chain that creates new green industries, good jobs and regional leadership for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is also an economic opportunity to secure Singapore's place as a leader in sustainable aviation innovation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: KLIA's Aeropolis Master Plan aims to handle over 100 million passengers a year.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Bangkok's Airport is expanding through a US$4 billion project.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Incheon Airport and Hong Kong International Airport's Three-Runway System will each soon handle up to 120 million passengers annually.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The proposed SAF levy, in addition to the levy that was already introduced, though small in absolute terms, could affect our price competitiveness, especially for transit traffic and air freight if neighbouring hubs delay similar moves.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Has the Ministry assessed the potential impact of this levy on Singapore's attractiveness as a transit and cargo hub?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And what mitigation strategies are being considered to preserve our competitiveness, while sustaining our leadership in sustainable aviation?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must ensure that environmental responsibility does not inadvertently erode our competitiveness as an international hub.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Instead, it should become a source of differentiation and trust.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But, within each flight, passengers pay vastly different fares across the different classes of flights.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ensuring fairness and transparency will be critical to maintaining public trust and broad-based support for this important transition.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is therefore important that we are clear about the levers and conditions that must be met before any price revisions are made, to ensure transparency, predictability and fairness.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ultimately, this is not a choice between economic growth and environmental stewardship, it is about advancing both, together, sustainably.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, I express my support for the Bill, which marks an important step in positioning Singapore as a global leader in sustainable and responsible aviation while creating good jobs, fostering innovation and ensuring that our skies and our future remain bright and green.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And he went on, "All of these predictions made by the United Nations and many others, often for bad reasons, were wrong.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But of course, their countries' fortunes, and given those same countries, no chance for success.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If you do not get away from this green scam, your country is going to fail." Given President Trump’s remarks and in the current context where cost-of-living continues to be of high concern, it may be attractive for countries worldwide to abandon our climate change strategies.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After all, if even the second largest emitter of carbon dioxide has decided to rubbish the endeavour, none of us alone will be able to move the needle – certainly not Singapore.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the other hand, there are some who say that our target is not ambitious enough.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They may quote regions like the EU, which I understand has agreed to rules mandating 6% in 2030, rising to 70% in 2050 and countries like Japan, which aims to have SAF account for 10% of its aviation fuel supply by 2030.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I note that the hon Member Mr Dennis Tan too, had asked last year if the Government will study plans by other countries with higher SAF targets such as Britain, Japan and the EU to raise our projected targets even further.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But today I heard he also said that he was conscious of the financial impact to travellers.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, perhaps we would invite him to clarify whether he is of the view where we should have higher targets and therefore higher levy on travellers or has he changed his mind with the concern of the financial impact on travellers today?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It connected me to people and cultures worldwide, to develop friendships which I know will last a lifetime.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It opened my mind to new sights, sounds and perspectives.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that many more in our current generation and future generations in Singapore and beyond Singapore will also be able to benefit from air travel.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Aviation is responsible for about 2.5% of global carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, estimates are that 80% of the global population, about 5 to 6 billion people worldwide, have never taken an air flight – and there will be some in Singapore as well.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The impact on the environment will be immense, and this may then severely constrain the options for future generations.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is why I believe we need to reduce emissions from air travel.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And based on current science, SAF is the most viable pathway to do so in the short and medium term.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Members have highlighted that Singapore's approach to introducing SAF is novel.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We are the first country to introduce a levy rather than a mandate.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: CAAS’ intent is to fix the cost of using greener jet fuel so that travellers have certainty.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: CAAS will also manage costs by procuring sustainable fuel centrally on behalf of carriers, reaping economies of scale.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some Members asked: would it be better to charge the airlines instead?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I am of the view that having a transparent charge to the travellers avoids the risk of airlines using this as a reason to inject further upward pressure on prices because of a lack of transparency.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, Sir, this approach protects both the environment and the competitiveness of Singapore’s air hub, a major economic sector for us.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It has at its heart the interests of both the current generation and future generations.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It may not have as ambitious a target as some other countries, but it is a target backed up by a robust plan as the Bill shows, implementable, deliverable, not just for show.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And may I add, while it is important that we understand, consider and assess the strategies taken by other countries, there must be occasions where our convictions give us the strength to take our own path.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And this is something that this Government has never shied away from.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But it is a commitment by all Singaporeans and all travellers who come through our airports to give hope to our future generations.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the words of Dr Jane Goodall: "And even today, when the planet is dark, there is still hope.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If you lose hope, you become apathetic and do nothing." Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Lee Hui Ying, Ms Gho Sze Kee, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the impact of the SAF levy on Singapore’s hub competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Singapore has chosen a pragmatic and balanced approach.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We are a council member of ICAO and are committed to working towards the ICAO's long-term aspirational goal of net zero carbon emissions for international aviation by 2050.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Airlines and passengers fly through Changi Airport for various reasons, including safety, network and connectivity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I just want to reply to the clarification which Member Mr Foo Cexiang sought.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Mr Foo is right, I had made certain clarifications on this issue with the previous Minister.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I heard the Minister with his explanation and I am prepared to let this Fund and the plans take off and see how we progress in the initial years and then we can take it from there.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any other clarifications for Senior Minister of State Sun?
